title: Building sentences: from A1 to almost A2
intro: Dutch word order follows a few firm rules. Learn them in order. Each rule has examples from your week, and the practice is mostly building sentences from word tiles.

notes.title: 1. The basic order: who, verb, the rest
body: A simple Dutch sentence starts like English. First comes the person or thing that does the action, then the verb, then everything else.

examples.en: I buy bread.
She swims on Wednesdays.

notes.title: 2. The verb always comes second
body: In a normal statement the verb is the second part of the sentence. If you start with something else, like a time or a place, the subject moves to just after the verb.
English says “Today she goes to school”. Dutch says “Today goes she to school”.
“Second part” is not always the second word. “Om drie uur” is one part, so the verb comes straight after it.

examples.en: She is going to school today.
Today she is going to school.

examples.nl: Om drie uur [haal] ik haar op.
examples.en: At three o'clock I pick her up.

links.label: Wikibooks Dutch, lesson 3: Word order and inversion

notes.title: 3. Questions: the verb comes first
body: For a yes-or-no question, start with the verb. With a question word such as wie, wat, waar, wanneer or hoe laat, the question word comes first and the verb second.
When je comes straight after the verb, the verb drops its -t. Je drinkt becomes drink je?

examples.en: Do you have a loyalty card?
Do you drink coffee?
Where is her coat?
What time does the lesson start?

notes.title: 4. Two verbs: the second goes to the end
body: With willen, kunnen, moeten, mogen and gaan, the first verb stays in second place. The main verb goes to the very end of the sentence, in its full form.

examples.en: I'd like to pay.
She has to get up early tomorrow.
We're going grocery shopping on Saturday.

links.label: Wikibooks Dutch, lesson 11: Verbs in final position

notes.title: 5. Split verbs: ophalen, meenemen, aandoen
body: Some verbs have a small front part, like op, mee or aan. In a simple sentence that front part moves to the end.
When the verb itself is already at the end, for example after wil or ga, the two parts stay together.

examples.en: I pick her up at three. (ophalen)
I'm bringing a bottle of water. (meenemen)

examples.nl: Ik ga haar om drie uur [ophalen].
examples.en: I'm going to pick her up at three.

notes.title: 6. The past: heb or ben, plus the past form at the end
body: To talk about something finished, put heb, hebt, heeft, ben or is in second place. The past form of the main verb goes to the end. It usually starts with ge-.
Use zijn (ben, is) for movement to a place and for a change of state. Use hebben for almost everything else.

examples.en: I bought bread.
She went to dance class.
She passed swimming diploma A.

notes.title: 7. Saying no: geen or niet
body: Use geen in front of a noun that would otherwise have een or no article. Use niet for everything else.
Niet usually goes near the end: before a place, before a describing word, or before the second verb.

examples.en: I don't have a bag.
She isn't coming today.
She isn't sick.
I can't come tomorrow.

links.label: Wikibooks Dutch, lesson 4: geen and niet

notes.title: 8. Towards A2: want and omdat both mean “because”
body: After want, keep the normal order: subject, then verb.
After omdat, the verb moves to the end of that part of the sentence. This is your first “side sentence”.

examples.nl: Ze blijft thuis, want ze [is] ziek.
examples.en: She's staying home, because she's sick.

examples.nl: Ze blijft thuis, omdat ze ziek [is].
examples.en: She's staying home, because she's sick.

links.label: Wikibooks Dutch, lesson 11: want and omdat
links.note: has a table of both kinds of linking words

notes.title: 9. Towards A2: dat, als, wanneer send the verb to the end
body: Words like dat (that), als (if or when), omdat and wanneer start a side sentence. In a side sentence the verb goes to the end.
If the side sentence comes first, the main sentence then starts with its verb. You get verb, comma, verb.

examples.en: I think she's tired.
Do you know when the lesson starts?

examples.nl: Als het [regent], [gaan] we met de auto.
examples.en: If it rains, we'll go by car.

cards.rule: Basic order: who, verb, the rest.
Basic order, or start with the time and keep the verb second.

cards.en: Today she is going to school.
cards.rule: Verb second: after “vandaag”, the verb comes before “ze”.

cards.nl: Om drie uur haal ik haar op.
cards.en: At three o'clock I pick her up.
alts: Ik haal haar om drie uur op.
cards.rule: Verb second, and “op” from ophalen goes to the end.
Verb second: “op zaterdag” is one part.

cards.en: Do you have a loyalty card?
cards.rule: Yes-or-no question: verb first.
Verb first, and the -t drops before je.
Question word first, verb second.

cards.en: What time does dance class start?
cards.rule: Question word first, verb second.
Two verbs: the second one goes to the end.

cards.en: She has to get up early tomorrow.
cards.rule: Two verbs: opstaan goes to the end, in one piece.

cards.en: We're going grocery shopping on Saturday.
cards.rule: gaan + verb at the end, for plans.

cards.en: Can you put your shoes on?
cards.rule: Question with two verbs: kun first, aandoen at the end.

cards.nl: Ik neem een fles water mee.
cards.en: I'm bringing a bottle of water.
cards.rule: Split verb: “mee” from meenemen goes to the end.
Split verb: “op” from opruimen goes to the end.
Past: heb second, gekocht at the end.

cards.nl: Ze is naar de dansles gegaan.
cards.rule: Past with zijn, because it is movement to a place.

cards.nl: Gisteren heeft ze een gele band gehaald.
cards.en: Yesterday she got her yellow belt.
alts: Ze heeft gisteren een gele band gehaald.
cards.rule: Past, plus verb second after “gisteren”.
geen before a noun with een or no article.
niet near the end.
niet before the second verb.

cards.nl: Ze blijft thuis, want ze is ziek.
cards.en: She's staying home, because she's sick. (use want)
cards.rule: want keeps the normal order.

cards.nl: We gaan met de fiets, omdat het mooi weer is.
cards.en: We're going by bike because the weather is nice. (use omdat)
alts: Omdat het mooi weer is, gaan we met de fiets.
cards.rule: omdat sends the verb to the end.

cards.nl: Ik denk dat ze moe is.
cards.rule: dat sends the verb to the end.

cards.nl: Weet u wanneer de les begint?
cards.en: Do you know when the lesson starts?
cards.rule: wanneer in the middle sends the verb to the end.

cards.nl: Als het regent, gaan we met de auto.
cards.en: If it rains, we'll go by car.
alts: We gaan met de auto als het regent.
cards.rule: Side sentence first, then verb, comma, verb.

cards.nl: Ze zegt dat ze honger heeft.
cards.rule: dat sends the verb to the end.
